record.paper_title: Eight Open Problems in Distributed Computing
record.context_brief: Pure Nash equilibria with link-capacity beliefs
record.original_question: In the incomplete-information extension of the KP selfish-routing model, where n selfish users route unsplittable traffic over m parallel links, links may have several possible capacities, and each user's belief about link capacities is a probability distribution that may differ from the beliefs of other users, does every instance admit a Pure Nash Equilibrium, or can the conjecture that such equilibria always exist be disproved?

evidence.quote: The problem of existence of pure Nash Equilibria for this new model in the general case is a non-trivial problem; as of this writing, it remains open.
It is conjectured that the model introduced in [38] always admits a Pure Nash equilibrium in general. Proving or disproving this conjecture is an interesting open challenge.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the following routing game with incomplete information about link capacities. There are $n$ selfish users and $m$ parallel links connecting a common source to a common destination. Each user $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ controls an unsplittable amount of traffic $w_i > 0$ that must be routed entirely on a single link. Each link $\ell \in \{1,\dots,m\}$ has a capacity drawn from a finite set $C_\ell = \{c_\ell^{(1)}, c_\ell^{(2)}, \dots, c_\ell^{(k_\ell)}\}$ of possible positive real values. For every user $i$ and every link $\ell$, user $i$ holds a subjective probability distribution $p_{i,\ell}$ on $C_\ell$ representing $i$'s belief about the capacity of link $\ell$; these beliefs may differ across users (the users' priors need not be common nor consistent). 

A (pure) strategy of user $i$ is a choice of one link $s_i \in \{1,\dots,m\}$. Given a pure strategy profile $s = (s_1,\dots,s_n)$, the expected cost (latency) experienced by user $i$ on link $\ell = s_i$, under $i$'s own belief, is
$$\mathrm{cost}_i(s) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{c \sim p_{i,\ell}}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{j:\, s_j = \ell} w_j}{c}\right].$$
A pure strategy profile $s^*$ is a Pure Nash Equilibrium if, for every user $i$ and every alternative link $\ell' \in \{1,\dots,m\}$,
$$\mathrm{cost}_i(s^*) \;\le\; \mathrm{cost}_i(s^*_{-i}, \ell').$$

Question: Does every instance of this game (for arbitrary $n$, $m$, weights $w_i$, capacity sets $C_\ell$, and user-specific belief distributions $p_{i,\ell}$) admit a Pure Nash Equilibrium? Either prove existence in full generality, or exhibit an instance with no Pure Nash Equilibrium.
artifact.status_search_result: Available literature on selfish routing under network uncertainty with user-specific (subjective) beliefs about link capacities indicates that existence of a Pure Nash Equilibrium in the general case is an open problem; negative results known for related models with three users do not apply here. Related Bayesian routing models with uncertainty about other users' traffic (not capacities) admit a potential-function argument guaranteeing pure Bayesian Nash equilibria, but this does not resolve the capacity-belief variant. No definitive proof or counterexample for the general capacity-belief KP model was located.

status_evidence.title: Selfish Routing in the Presence of Network Uncertainty (Parallel Processing Letters)
status_evidence.snippet: Combines the KP-model with user-specific belief functions; existence of pure Nash equilibria in the general case posed as open; known non-existence results with three users do not apply.
status_evidence.claim: Existence of pure Nash equilibria in the capacity-belief KP model remains stated as open in the general case.

status_evidence.title: Selfish Routing with Incomplete Information (Theory of Computing Systems)
status_evidence.snippet: Every Bayesian routing game (incomplete information about user traffic) admits a pure Bayesian Nash equilibrium via a potential function.
status_evidence.claim: A different incomplete-information variant (uncertainty about users' types) is fully resolved, but not the capacity-beliefs variant in question.
